misconceptions.statement: One company or government owns and controls the whole internet.
misconceptions.why: Students see a few big brands like Google and Jio and assume they run everything.
misconceptions.fix: The internet is thousands of separate networks run by companies, governments and universities that agree to connect using common rules. No one owner controls all of it.

probe.question: Who owns the internet?
probe.wrong_answer: Google (or the government) owns it.

misconceptions.root_belief: big visible things have one owner in charge

misconceptions.statement: The internet is a single giant computer somewhere.
misconceptions.why: People talk about 'the net' as one place or thing.
misconceptions.fix: The internet is a huge number of computers and devices joined by cables and radio links. There is no single central computer.

probe.question: Where is the internet located?
probe.wrong_answer: In one huge central computer.

misconceptions.root_belief: one name means one single object
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' mental models of the internet in computing education research

misconceptions.statement: A router makes the internet; without it the internet does not exist.
misconceptions.why: Home internet stops when the router is off, so it seems to create the internet.
misconceptions.fix: A router only passes data between your devices and other networks. The internet itself is the worldwide set of connected networks.

probe.question: A router is the source of internet. True or false?
probe.wrong_answer: True, the router produces the internet.

misconceptions.root_belief: the device I touch is the source of everything

misconceptions.statement: Wi-Fi and the internet are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Phones show 'Wi-Fi' as the way to get online, so the words are used interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: Wi-Fi is a radio link between your device and a router. A Wi-Fi network can exist with no internet connection at all.

probe.question: Your Wi-Fi is connected but no website opens. What is wrong?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing, Wi-Fi connected means the internet is working.

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: computing education research on learners confusing Wi-Fi, web and internet

misconceptions.statement: Internet data is free because it just exists in the air; ISPs only fix wires.
misconceptions.why: Students never see the infrastructure cost behind the connection.
misconceptions.fix: An ISP owns or rents cables and equipment that connect you to the wider internet, and charges for that access.

probe.question: Why do we pay an ISP every month?
probe.wrong_answer: For nothing real, the internet is already in the air.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not cost anything

misconceptions.statement: The World Wide Web and the internet are the same thing.
misconceptions.why: Everyday speech uses 'net' and 'web' interchangeably.
misconceptions.fix: The internet is the network of connected devices; the web is one service on it, made of web pages. Email and video calls also use the internet without being the web.

probe.question: Is email part of the web or the internet?
probe.wrong_answer: Email is the web, because the web is the internet.

misconceptions.root_belief: two related terms mean the same thing
misconceptions.source_hint: research on school students' conceptions of internet versus web

misconceptions.statement: Only computers and phones have IP addresses; a smart TV or CCTV camera does not.
misconceptions.why: Students link addresses with obvious computing devices.
misconceptions.fix: Any device that connects to a network, such as a TV, camera or smartwatch, gets an IP address to be found.

probe.question: Does a Wi-Fi CCTV camera need an IP address?
probe.wrong_answer: No, only computers do.

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule applies only to the typical example

misconceptions.statement: An IP address tells exactly which house a person lives in.
misconceptions.why: The word 'address' suggests a home address, and crime shows reinforce it.
misconceptions.fix: An IP address identifies a connection on a network and can change; it usually shows only a rough area of the provider, not a house.

probe.question: If you know someone's IP address, can you find their exact flat?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it gives the exact house location.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of misconceptions about IP addresses and online privacy

misconceptions.statement: You must type the numbers of an IP address to reach a website; names like google.com are the real address.
misconceptions.why: Students only ever see names, so names seem to be the actual address.
misconceptions.fix: Computers find websites using IP numbers. DNS works like a phone book that looks up the number for the name you type.

probe.question: What does DNS do when you type a website name?
probe.wrong_answer: Nothing; the name itself directly points to the website.

misconceptions.root_belief: what I see is all that is happening

misconceptions.statement: A video or photo travels over the internet as one single block.
misconceptions.why: A file looks like one object on screen, so students assume it moves whole.
misconceptions.fix: Files are cut into many small packets, each with the destination address, and sent separately.

probe.question: How does a large photo get sent to a friend?
probe.wrong_answer: The whole photo moves as one piece along one path.

misconceptions.root_belief: things move the way they look
misconceptions.source_hint: research on learners' mental models of data transmission

misconceptions.statement: All packets of a message follow the same path and arrive in order.
misconceptions.why: Students imagine one fixed road like a pipe or a train line.
misconceptions.fix: Each packet may take a different route and arrive out of order; the receiving device puts them back in order.

probe.question: Two packets of one message take different routes. What happens?
probe.wrong_answer: This cannot happen; all must use the same path.

misconceptions.root_belief: one fixed path connects start and end
misconceptions.source_hint: studies of students' pipe or direct-line models of the internet

misconceptions.statement: Most internet data between countries goes through satellites.
misconceptions.why: Satellites are famous in news and space lessons, while cables are hidden under the sea.
misconceptions.fix: About 95 percent or more of international data travels through undersea fibre-optic cables; satellites carry only a small share.

probe.question: How does a video call from India to the USA mostly travel?
probe.wrong_answer: Through satellites in space.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: surveys of public and student beliefs about internet infrastructure

misconceptions.statement: Undersea cables carry data as electricity in copper wires or as radio waves.
misconceptions.why: Students know wires from electricity lessons and assume all cables carry current.
misconceptions.fix: Undersea internet cables use hair-thin glass fibres that carry data as pulses of light.

probe.question: What carries data inside an undersea internet cable?
probe.wrong_answer: Electric current in copper wire.

misconceptions.root_belief: a familiar rule from one topic works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: Mobile phones connect to the internet directly through satellites, with no towers needed.
misconceptions.why: Phone signals feel wireless and 'from the sky'.
misconceptions.fix: A phone sends radio signals to a nearby mobile tower, which is joined to the wired network by cables.

probe.question: What does your phone connect to when you open a website on mobile data?
probe.wrong_answer: A satellite directly above.

misconceptions.root_belief: wireless means nothing physical is involved
misconceptions.source_hint: research on students' ideas of wireless communication

misconceptions.statement: Wireless internet needs no wires anywhere; the whole path is through the air.
misconceptions.why: The word 'wireless' is taken to apply to the whole journey.
misconceptions.fix: Wireless covers only the last hop from device to tower or router. After that, data travels through wires and fibre cables.

probe.question: Is any wire used when you browse on mobile data?
probe.wrong_answer: No wires at all, everything is in the air.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: computing education studies on learners' mental models of wireless networks

misconceptions.statement: A server is a special kind of machine different from ordinary computers.
misconceptions.why: The word 'server' sounds like exotic technology.
misconceptions.fix: A server is a computer running software that answers requests; it is usually more powerful and runs all the time.

probe.question: Can an ordinary laptop work as a server?
probe.wrong_answer: No, servers are a completely different kind of machine.

misconceptions.root_belief: special names mean special kinds of thing

misconceptions.statement: A website's pages are stored on your own phone or are just floating in the internet.
misconceptions.why: Pages appear instantly, so they seem to be already here or everywhere.
misconceptions.fix: A website's files are stored on a server. Your browser requests them and shows a copy.

probe.question: Where is a website stored?
probe.wrong_answer: In the internet itself, or on my phone.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: studies on learners' beliefs about where web content lives

misconceptions.statement: The cloud is data floating in the sky or a magical space with no physical place.
misconceptions.why: The word 'cloud' and its icon suggest something in the air.
misconceptions.fix: The cloud means computers owned by other companies in large buildings called data centres, which you use over the internet.

probe.question: Where are your cloud photos really kept?
probe.wrong_answer: Up in the air in a cloud.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning
misconceptions.source_hint: research on public and student understanding of cloud storage

misconceptions.statement: Photos saved in the cloud can never be lost or deleted.
misconceptions.why: Cloud seems permanent and unlimited.
misconceptions.fix: Cloud data can be lost if an account is closed, deleted by mistake or hacked, so important files need backups.

probe.question: Do you need another copy of an important file saved in the cloud?
probe.wrong_answer: No, the cloud always keeps it safe forever.

misconceptions.root_belief: unseen things are perfectly safe and permanent

misconceptions.statement: Faster internet always means the website's server is nearby.
misconceptions.why: Students think speed depends only on distance.
misconceptions.fix: Speed depends on many things: your connection, network traffic and server load, not only distance.

probe.question: A site loads slowly even though the server is in your city. Why?
probe.wrong_answer: Impossible; nearby servers are always fast.

misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: Sending data over the internet uses up the data like fuel, so it disappears from my device.
misconceptions.why: Mobile 'data packs' are described as being used up.
misconceptions.fix: Sending a file only copies it; the original stays with you. A data pack counts how much data is transferred.

probe.question: After you email a photo, is it still on your phone?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it has moved and is gone.

misconceptions.root_belief: sending something means you no longer have it
